prize_parts.citation: for introducing firm heterogeneity and selection into the theory of international trade, and thereby changing how the gains from trade and their reallocation effects are understood and measured

statement.case_for: B001 is the discovery where I see the largest and cleanest conceptual shift that has also been tested for a long time. Melitz (2003) and Helpman-Melitz-Yeaple (2004) moved trade analysis from industries to firms. They explain who exports and who invests abroad, and they identify reallocation across firms as a distinct channel for gains from trade. The idea reorganised theory, empirical work on firm microdata and policy evaluation, and it also reached macro and productivity research. It has been checked in many countries and datasets over more than twenty years. As an economic historian, I value work that changes what we measure and how we understand what we measure, and this framework did that. Eleven opening rankings from members with different specialisations point to the same candidate. I treat that only as a sign that the field assessment is not idiosyncratic, not as evidence of merit. The two-name attribution is defensible on the record. Melitz supplies the canonical selection model, and Helpman supplies the foundations of differentiated-product trade theory plus the exporting-versus-FDI margin.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is attribution. The ballot credits three names, and I propose two. Redding's quantitative and spatial extensions are very influential, so the committee could regard leaving him out as too narrow. Separately, Bernard, Eaton, Jensen and Kortum made closely related contributions, including the empirical facts on exporter premia, and they are outside the credited set. Cleanly dating the discovery therefore carries real risk. A second concern is that the baseline model's sharper predictions are rejected in detail. Its welfare implications also depend on functional-form and distributional assumptions, so the citation should claim a new framework and research agenda and not a settled measure of the gains from trade. I have not independently verified the priority record beyond what the colleagues' openings and my own knowledge support.

responses.point: Andersson ranks B001 first with Helpman and Melitz. He sees Melitz as originator of the core heterogeneous-firm model and Helpman as the broadest foundational contributor. He treats Redding as a later extension that is less central to this discovery, and he flags that the committee may want a three-person split or a different pairing.
responses.response: I agree on the core attribution and have reached the same two names independently. I would qualify it in one respect. My own research interests in regional and spatial growth make me more attentive to Redding's quantitative-spatial work than I would otherwise be, and I have tested whether that is skewing my view. I conclude that his contribution builds on the selection framework and does not originate it. I would still make the citation explicit that it covers the selection and reallocation framework, so that it does not read as a verdict on the whole quantitative trade literature. That wording also answers the worry that a two-name award leaves out a plausible third name.

responses.point: Hassler ranks the BLP demand-estimation and dynamic-industry framework (B006) first and B001 second. He argues that the methods are fully mature, are cleanly attributable to Berry, Levinsohn and Pakes, and have large applied reach in merger review, antitrust and other policy fields. He acknowledges that Bresnahan and Reiss complicate the boundary.
responses.response: This is the strongest challenge to my first place, and it has moved B006 into my alternatives. I accept that the BLP attribution is arguably tidier than B001's, because the Bernard-Eaton-Jensen-Kortum parallel work is not a comparable problem there. I also accept the maturity and the breadth of use. Where I still differ is the kind of contribution. B001 changed the conceptual account of a major economic phenomenon, and B006 is mainly a transferable estimation toolkit, though a very influential one. That distinction is not sharp, and I do not want to turn it into a rule. If the committee prefers tool-building with demonstrated practical reach, I would treat B006 as a serious option. I would then want the committee to settle first whether demand estimation and the dynamic-games strand are one discovery or two.

responses.point: Boppart ranks B001 first. He stresses that the shift from sectors to firms is broad in reach and mature. He also notes that Bernard, Eaton, Jensen and Kortum are important parallel contributors outside the credited set, and that Krugman's earlier prize covered part of the new-trade-theory lineage.
responses.response: I agree that the Krugman overlap should discipline the wording, and I would add that the citation should say nothing generic about trade theory. It should name selection and firm heterogeneity. That keeps the award separate from the 2008 recognition. On Bernard, Eaton, Jensen and Kortum, I am less comfortable than you may be with treating them as only a caveat. If the committee reads the discovery as the empirical facts plus the theory, the ballot's credited names would be incomplete. My answer is that the prize recognises the model that organised those facts and generated the new welfare channel, which is where Melitz and Helpman's claim rests. I acknowledge this is a judgment about what counts as the discovery, and I do not think the record settles it.

responses.point: Krusell ranks B034 second. He treats the Kiyotaki-Moore collateral-constraint mechanism as a clean two-person attribution. He is wary of extending credit to Gertler and Gilchrist because the accelerator line overlaps with the 2022 prize.
responses.response: We agree on this, and B034 is also my second choice. I would add that the overlap with 2022 cuts both ways. It reduces perceived novelty, but a prize explicitly tied to the dynamic collateral-constraint mechanism, and not to financial frictions generally, would be distinguishable. My remaining doubt is that the empirical identification of the collateral channel is indirect. That is a real difference in evidential maturity from B001, whose predictions have been tested directly in firm-level data. I would therefore keep B034 as an alternative and not as my first choice.

uncertainties: Whether Redding should be added as a third laureate, and whether the Bernard-Eaton-Jensen-Kortum contributions outside the credited names make the two-name attribution too narrow.
Whether the committee reads the discovery as the selection model plus its empirical agenda, or as a family of trade-and-firms contributions.
How strongly the dependence of the baseline model's welfare implications on distributional assumptions should limit the wording of the citation.
Whether B006 deserves priority over B001 if the committee weights transferable methods with large applied reach above a conceptual reorientation.
How much the overlap of B034 with the 2022 prize, and of B030 with recent prizes on labour and on technology and growth, should count against those candidates.
statement.conflict_note: None apparent from the supplied profile. The profile lists no collaboration, supervision or institutional tie to any credited candidate on the shortlist. My field is economic history, with work on regional growth, infrastructure and labour markets. That gives me some interest in spatial and quantitative extensions (Redding) and in labour-market adjustment (B030), which I disclose as thematic proximity and not as a personal connection. Colleagues from Lund and Johannes Lindvall as a co-author are not candidates.
